Hanul lui Manuc · Bucharest · 1808

A courtyard
for a continent.

Une cour pour un continent.

A boy from the Danube grew into Manuc Bey: Armenian merchant, Ottoman diplomat, and host to the room in which empires changed the map.

Enter the courtyard ↓

Bucharest, 1808

01

A capital of
strangers.

A city of around eighty thousand, more than half born elsewhere. Greek in the coffee houses. Armenian in the jewellery shops. German in the workshops. Bulgarian in the cloth warehouses. French at the prince’s table. Romanian, at last, on the street.

Une capitale d’arrivées : les langues de l’Europe et du Levant se croisent avant même que la Roumanie ne devienne un État.

The man

Emanuel
Mârzaian.

Born in Ruse in 1769, in the Ottoman port then called Rustchuk, he arrived in Iași at twelve in the service of an Armenian merchant. Romanian first; then French; then Russian. Within a few years, contemporaries said he could move between a dozen languages.

His name travelled with him: merchant, banker, paharnic, Grand Dragoman of the Sublime Porte, and finally Manuc Bey of Moldavia. He never ruled the principality. But he knew how to make a place where those who did might speak.

A life in motion

  1. 1769Ruse / Rustchuk
  2. c. 1781Iași
  3. 1807Grand Dragoman
  4. 1808Hanul lui Manuc
  5. 1812Treaty of Bucharest

The old title for the indispensable person between languages: dragoman.

The city arrives at the gate

Its streets kept
the guest list.

Lipscanimerchants returning from Leipzig
Gabrovenicloth merchants from Gabrovo
Șelarisaddlers
Covaciblacksmiths
Blănarifurriers
Zarafimoney-changers

The inn did not stand beside an abstract crossroads. It stood inside an operating one: horses, textiles, letters, currencies, officials and gossip, all looking for a roof.

The continent at the door

02

The room
becomes a frontier.

The war between Russia and the Ottoman Empire had run through the principalities since 1806. Beyond it lay the calculations of Napoleon, Alexander I, Constantinople and Paris. Bucharest was a listening post, a rear base, and a city under pressure.

For five months in 1811–12, Russian and Ottoman delegates met under Manuc’s roof. Kutuzov stood behind one side; Galib efendi led the other. The courtyard that had made room for travellers was now making room for peace.

28 May 1812

The Treaty of Bucharest is signed at Manuc’s Inn.

13 days later Napoleon’s Grande Armée crosses the Niemen.

On this map Russia takes the eastern half of Moldavia, between the Prut and Dniester: the territory soon called Bessarabia.

For Romania a merchant’s room begins an argument that will outlast the empires around it.

What remains

The shape
of continuity.

Manuc died in 1817. The inn became a hotel, a theatre, a meeting place for Greater Romania, a nationalised property, and again a family property. The treaty was replaced by other treaties; the empires by successor states.

But the galleries still ring a courtyard. The oak columns still carry rooms above the street. In a city rebuilt and renamed many times, that is not nothing.

To face west does not require
forgetting the road behind.Se tourner vers l’Ouest ne demande pas d’oublier la route parcourue.
